topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Abstract Factory creates related products through one chosen family provider. Worked example: Plain and framed digit codec families. CodecFactory groups two independent creation operations under one family choice. round_trip depends only on factory and product interfaces, and explicitly checks the compatibility invariant.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Construct related products from one chosen family.
Explain why interfaces alone do not prove compatibility.
Test encoding and decoding together, including rejected cross-family input.

blocks.text: Declare an interface for each product role and a factory interface with one creation operation per role. Each concrete factory implements every operation for one family. Pass one selected factory to the client; let the client request its products through that factory. The return types hide concrete classes. Compatibility remains a behavior contract: an incorrect factory can return mismatched implementations while satisfying the C++ types.

cards.question: What problem does Abstract Factory address?
cards.answer: Abstract Factory creates related products through one chosen family provider. Worked example: Plain and framed digit codec families. CodecFactory groups two independent creation operations under one family choice. round_trip depends only on factory and product interfaces, and explicitly checks the compatibility invariant.

cards.question: What is Abstract Factory?
cards.answer: An interface for creating the different product roles in one compatible family.

cards.question: What is Round trip?
cards.answer: Writing a value and then reading it back to verify that its meaning is preserved.

cards.question: What is Short-circuit evaluation?
cards.answer: Skipping the remaining part of a logical expression when the result is already decided.

cards.question: Why can a faulty FramedFactory returning PlainDecoder still compile?
cards.answer: PlainDecoder implements Decoder, so the return type matches. C++ checks the interface; the round-trip tests check the family behavior.

cards.question: Which change affects every factory: adding another family or adding a third product role?
cards.answer: Adding a third role adds a factory operation each family must implement. A new family can implement the existing factory interface without changing existing families.

cards.question: Two encoders emit identical bytes today. Must their decoders be interchangeable forever?
cards.answer: No. Matching a few outputs does not establish the whole protocol contract. Test the complete supported input domain and malformed inputs before claiming interchangeability.

cards.question: Where should a client choose the codec family for one session?
cards.answer: Choose one factory at the session boundary and obtain both products from it. Choosing each product independently makes accidental mixed families easier.

cards.question: Would one encode/decode object be simpler than two product interfaces?
cards.answer: Yes, if clients always need both together and neither varies independently. Abstract Factory is useful when several related products must be supplied through separate roles.

cards.question: Why test all ten digits instead of only seven?
cards.answer: The domain is tiny, so exhaustive valid-input checks are cheap. They catch endpoint and off-by-one defects that a single demonstration misses.

cards.question: Does a unique_ptr<Decoder> express protocol compatibility?
cards.answer: No. It expresses ownership and the Decoder interface. Family compatibility remains a design rule enforced by factory construction and tests.

cards.question: What should happen to d=04 in this chapter's protocol?
cards.answer: Reject it. The supported tagged form has exactly one digit, so accepting an extra zero silently broadens the language beyond the stated contract.

cards.question: How can a new family be added without editing round_trip?
cards.answer: Implement matching Encoder and Decoder products plus a CodecFactory. round_trip depends on those interfaces and checks that decoding recovers the original digit.

topics.summary: A small teaching protocol transmits one decimal digit, from 0 through 9. A plain connection sends 7 as the string 7. A framed connection sends the same value as [7]. Each connection needs two objects: an encoder that writes a digit and a decoder that reads the resulting string. Every accepted digit must survive the trip unchanged. Invalid numbers and malformed strings must be rejected.

discussion.question: Why is choosing an encoder and decoder independently risky, even when each one works alone?
discussion.answer: Their wire formats may disagree. A framed encoder can produce [7] while a plain decoder expects 7. The requirement is a matching pair, not merely two individually valid objects.

topics.title: The failure is a mismatched pair
topics.summary: When framed connections arrive, setup code selects both products independently. A copied branch can create FramedEncoder with PlainDecoder. Both objects implement the right C++ interfaces, so the compiler accepts the code. The encoder produces [7], but the plain decoder rejects its length. A more permissive decoder might silently misread the data instead. The problem is agreement between products, not merely selecting one product.

blocks.text: A family is a set of objects meant to work together. The Abstract Factory pattern gives the caller one object that creates all needed members of the selected family. CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder. PlainFactory creates the plain pair; FramedFactory creates the framed pair. The client chooses one factory, then asks that factory for both products. This reduces the number of places where incompatible choices can enter.

topics.title: Two product roles are not one inheritance tree
topics.summary: Encoder and Decoder have different operations, so they remain different interfaces. PlainEncoder and FramedEncoder implement Encoder. PlainDecoder and FramedDecoder implement Decoder. Each concrete factory creates one of each. Abstract Factory does not require these two products to inherit from each other, share a common catch-all interface, or own one another. Their useful relationship is a protocol contract: decoder.read(encoder.write(value)) equals value for every valid value.

blocks.text: The factory itself is borrowed as const CodecFactory&. The client does not delete it and does not save its address. Each returned unique_ptr owns a fresh product. The products contain no reference back to the factory, so this implementation does not require them to die before the factory. In round_trip they are local and are destroyed when the call ends. A different implementation with shared factory state would need a documented lifetime rule instead of assuming this one applies.

The compiler checks product method signatures and factory overrides. During execution, the actual factory type chooses the concrete products. Calling through Encoder and Decoder then chooses their actual method implementations. The client contains no switch on wire format. It still knows the abstract protocol duties: one writer, one reader, a valid integer, and a round-trip invariant.

topics.title: Parsing is part of the contract
topics.summary: PlainDecoder checks that wire has exactly one character before testing its content. The || operator stops as soon as an operand is true. This short-circuit rule skips unnecessary content tests after a bad length. FramedDecoder uses the same ordering for a stronger safety reason: front() and back() require a nonempty string. Its size check rejects empty input before either operation can run. C++17 permits reading string[string.size()] as a zero character, so PlainDecoder’s wire[0] on an empty string is not the same invalid-access case as front() or back().

blocks.text: The character tests compare the input with '0' and '9'. C++ guarantees the decimal digit characters form a consecutive sequence, so subtracting '0' from a checked digit yields its numeric value. The framed reader first checks a three-character shape with opening and closing brackets. Only then does it take the one-character substring and reuse PlainDecoder. That reuse is a local parsing dependency, not membership in the plain factory family.

The encoder checks numeric range before making a string. The framed decoder rejects [x] even though its outer brackets are correct. Structural validity and content validity are different rules. These deliberately tiny formats let the tests cover all ten accepted numeric values. They are teaching protocols, not general-purpose serialization formats with escaping, byte-order rules, versioning, or checksums.

topics.title: A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it
topics.summary: Nothing in the return types prevents a faulty FramedFactory from returning PlainDecoder. The family rule is a design contract backed by tests. round_trip checks the value after decoding. That catches mismatches or broken decoding for the tested values. It cannot certify all future protocol extensions by itself. If a family has many configuration values, test representative boundaries and generated cases, and consider carrying a shared immutable configuration object into both products.

blocks.text: A factory is most useful when clients need several related product roles and whole families change together. Adding a new family is local: provide its products and a factory implementing the existing creation operations. Adding a new product role is less local: a new creation method affects every factory and every family. This is the pattern’s main change-direction tradeoff. Choose it when new families are more likely than new roles.

For one encoder-decoder pair with no planned variants, direct construction is clearer. A function returning a struct containing both owning handles can also preserve pairing with less inheritance. Compile-time family types or a single codec object can enforce stronger relationships when runtime variation is unnecessary. Do not split one naturally cohesive codec into separate products solely to make an Abstract Factory diagram. Here separate send and receive components are the stated need; the factory coordinates their creation.

topics.title: Exercise 02.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: The team will add ten new protocol families but expects encoder and decoder to remain the only roles. Explain why this change direction supports Abstract Factory, and what requirement would weaken that choice.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Count which interfaces change for a family versus a role.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: A new family implements the existing two methods and adds its own products, leaving callers stable. Frequently adding roles such as validator, compressor, and signer would force all factories to change, making a smaller family configuration object or another composition scheme worth considering. A strong answer ties the choice to expected change, not to the number of classes.

workshop.title: Plain and framed digit codec families
workshop.problem: Plain and framed digit codec families. Round-trip every digit from 0 through 9 in either family. Reject numbers outside the supported range and malformed wire strings. Create both products from one selected factory and own them locally.
workshop.output:
plain=7
framed=[7]
mixed family, range, and bad digit rejected

steps.why: The application chooses a whole family.
Both creation calls use that factory.
The writer validates the digit and adds its frame.
The reader checks brackets and enclosed digit before converting.

workshop.pitfall: Pair the framed writer with the plain reader. Writing 7 produces [7], which the plain reader rejects. Matching interface types do not imply matching wire formats.

discussion.question: One application always sends and reads through the same object. Another hands separate writer and reader objects to independent components and supports several format families. Choose a single codec or Abstract Factory.
discussion.answer: The first can use one Codec with write and read methods, eliminating pairing. The second can use Abstract Factory to create compatible separate roles from one choice. Both are sound when their object boundaries match the actual application.
discussion.hint: Look for a real need for separately created related objects.

workshop.alternative: A single Codec type with write and read methods avoids pairing entirely if send and receive need not be separate objects. A simple function returning an owning pair is also sufficient for a small closed set of families.
workshop.design: CodecFactory groups two independent creation operations under one family choice. round_trip depends only on factory and product interfaces, and explicitly checks the compatibility invariant.
invariants: For each supported digit, read(write(value)) equals value within one family.
Products returned by the supplied factories are non-null.
Decoders check structure before indexing or extracting content.
workshop.maintenance: Choose a family at the application boundary and pass that choice inward. New transport variants can then reuse the round-trip workflow and its checks instead of adding independent switches throughout the code.
workshop.verification: main tests both displayed forms and all ten valid digits for each family, rejects a mixed pair, rejects 10, and rejects [x]. The client checks non-null handles. Tests do not model transport loss, Unicode, large numbers, or a production serialization protocol.
